title: Palindrome Partitioning
directAnswer: Return every way to cut the string so that every piece is a palindrome. The canonical answer is backtracking with a start index: from `start`, try every cut end; if `s[start..end]` is a palindrome, choose that prefix, recurse from `end + 1`, then un-choose. Record the path when `start` reaches the end of the string. Optionally precompute an `isPalindrome[i][j]` DP table so each palindrome check is O(1) instead of O(n).

remember.pattern: Backtracking over cut points + palindrome check (choose → explore → un-choose)
remember.formula:
def backtrack(start, path):
    if start == len(s): results.append(path[:]); return
    for end in range(start, len(s)):
        if is_palindrome(start, end):          # only cut where the prefix is a palindrome
            path.append(s[start:end+1])        # choose this palindromic prefix
            backtrack(end + 1, path)           # explore the remainder
            path.pop()                         # un-choose
rules: Branch on the **cut point**: from `start`, every `end ≥ start` is a candidate prefix `s[start..end]`.
Only recurse when the prefix is a **palindrome** — that's the pruning that keeps the tree small and the answers valid.
Recurse from `end + 1` (the character after the cut), never from `start` — each character belongs to exactly one piece.
Record when `start == len(s)` — reaching the end means every character has been consumed by some palindromic piece.
Append a **copy** `path[:]` of the list of substrings — the live path is mutated on backtrack.
Precompute `isPalindrome[i][j]` with DP (or expand-around-center) to turn each check from O(n) into **O(1)** — a strong optimisation to mention.
whenToUse: Asked for **all** ways to split a string under a per-piece predicate (here: palindrome)
Each character must land in exactly one contiguous piece
The predicate (palindrome) can be checked on a substring quickly
You need the partitions themselves, not just a count or a minimum
antiSignals: Only the **minimum number of cuts** is needed → Palindrome Partitioning II, pure DP (don't enumerate)
Only the **count** of valid partitions → DP over indices, not backtracking
Pieces can overlap or be reordered → it's not a contiguous partition problem
String is huge → exponential partitions make full enumeration intractable
remember.takeaway: Palindrome Partitioning is the 'partition a sequence' member of the backtracking family: instead of choosing elements, you choose cut points, and a predicate (palindrome) prunes invalid cuts. The choose/explore/un-choose skeleton is identical to Subsets — only the branching (cut positions) and the prune (palindrome check) change. Adding an isPalindrome DP table is the canonical hybrid that earns it the dynamic-programming tag.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model the problem as choosing cut points (not elements), prune branches with a palindrome check, and correctly advance the recursion to `end + 1`. Bonus: precomputing the palindrome table with DP to make checks O(1) and quoting the right complexity.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recursing from `start` or `end` instead of `end + 1` (overlapping or skipped characters), re-checking palindromes naively inside the hot loop (slower than needed), or forgetting to copy the path so all partitions corrupt.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the cut-point model and the choose/explore/un-choose template, prune with the palindrome check, then offer the isPalindrome[i][j] DP precomputation, explaining how it drops each check to O(1) and giving the O(n · 2ⁿ) bound.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, partition `s` such that **every substring of the partition is a palindrome**. Return **all possible palindrome partitionings** of `s`.

A **palindrome** is a string that reads the same forward and backward.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
understanding: Split s into contiguous pieces so each piece reads the same forwards and backwards, and return every such splitting. A single character is always a palindrome, so the all-singletons partition is always valid — that guarantees at least one answer. We return the partitions (lists of substrings), not a count or a minimum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a single character considered a palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Any length-1 substring is trivially a palindrome, so splitting into all single characters is always a valid partition — there is always at least one answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the pieces have to be contiguous and cover the whole string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it's a partition: pieces are contiguous, non-overlapping, and together they spell s exactly. That's why we recurse from `end + 1` and stop when start reaches the end.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of the partitions in the output matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Any order of the partitionings is accepted. Within a partition, order is fixed because pieces are contiguous left-to-right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How long can s get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most 16 characters. The number of partitions can be up to 2¹⁵, so exponential enumeration is expected; the palindrome prune keeps real inputs fast.

examples.explanation: Cut after position 0 then 1 gives ["a","a","b"]; cutting "aa" (a palindrome) then "b" gives ["aa","b"]. "aab" itself isn't a palindrome, so no single-piece partition.
A single character is a palindrome, so the only partition is ["a"].
All singletons work, and the whole string "aba" is itself a palindrome, so it forms a one-piece partition too.

diagrams.title: The cut-point recursion tree
diagrams.caption: Each node is a position `start`; each edge picks a palindromic prefix and jumps to the character after it. Branches whose prefix isn't a palindrome are pruned (red). Reaching the end of the string is a winning leaf (green).

approaches.name: Backtracking over Cut Points (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Phrase it as 'at each position try every prefix; if it's a palindrome, take it and recurse on the rest — choose/explore/un-choose'.
hints: Think of inserting cut bars between characters. From the current position, what are your choices for where the NEXT piece ends?
From `start`, let `end` range over every position ≥ start. The prefix `s[start..end]` is a candidate piece — but you only want to recurse into it when it's a palindrome.
Choose the palindromic prefix (append the substring), explore the remainder by recursing from `end + 1`, then un-choose (pop). When `start` reaches the end of the string, record a copy of the path.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are up to 2^(n−1) ways to place cut bars, so up to O(2ⁿ) partitions in the worst case (e.g. "aaaa…"). Building/copying each partition costs O(n). With an O(1) palindrome check the total is O(n · 2ⁿ). Extra space beyond the output is the recursion depth and the path, both O(n) (plus O(n²) if you precompute the palindrome table).
approaches.explanation:
Model the problem as choosing **where to cut**. At each recursion level we sit at position `start` and decide where the next piece ends: let `end` sweep from `start` to the end of the string. For each `end`, the candidate piece is `s[start..end]`. We only descend into a cut when that piece is a **palindrome** — otherwise the branch can never yield a valid partition, so we skip it. We **choose** the piece (append the substring), **explore** the rest of the string by recursing from `end + 1`, then **un-choose** (pop). When `start == len(s)`, every character has been swallowed by some palindromic piece, so the current path is a complete valid partition and we record a copy.

**Why we branch on cut points, not on elements.** Subsets and permutations choose *which elements* to include; here the elements (characters) are all used and in fixed order — the only freedom is *where the boundaries fall*. So the branching factor at position `start` is 'how long is the next piece', i.e. the choice of `end`. That reframing is the whole modelling insight: a partition problem is a 'choose the next boundary' backtracking problem.

**Why the palindrome check is the prune.** Without it we'd enumerate all 2^(n−1) ways to cut and filter at the end — but a cut that makes a non-palindromic prefix can *never* be completed into a valid answer, so we reject it immediately and never explore its subtree. This is classic backtracking pruning: test the constraint as early as possible (right at the cut) so dead branches die instantly. For "aab", the prefix "ab" fails the test, so the entire subtree under 'first piece = ab' is skipped.

**Why we recurse from `end + 1` (not `start`, not `end`).** Each character must belong to exactly one piece. After committing `s[start..end]` as a piece, the *next* piece must begin at the very next character, `end + 1`. Recursing from `start` would re-cut characters we already placed (overlap); recursing from `end` would re-use `s[end]` in two pieces. The `+1` is what makes the pieces a clean partition that tiles the string.

**Why record at `start == len(s)` and copy the path.** Reaching the end means the cuts we made consumed the whole string with palindromic pieces — a complete answer. We snapshot `path[:]` because `path` is shared and mutated by the pops as we backtrack; appending the live list would leave every stored partition pointing at the same, later-emptied list. The always-valid all-singletons partition falls out naturally because every single character passes the palindrome test.
approaches.insight: The choose/explore/un-choose skeleton here is byte-for-byte the same as Subsets — what changes is the branching (cut positions instead of element indices) and the prune (palindrome test instead of 'always allowed'). Recognising that 'partition a sequence under a per-piece predicate' maps onto the same template lets you reuse one mental model for Palindrome Partitioning, Word Break II, and Restore IP Addresses.

dryRun.intro: From each `start`, sweep `end`; only descend when s[start..end] is a palindrome. Recurse from end+1. Record when start reaches 3 (end of string).

steps.action: try end=1: "aa" palindrome → choose, recurse from 2
"b" palindrome → record; ("aab" at start=0 not a palindrome → pruned)

java.explanation: Base case: start reaching the end means every character was consumed by a palindromic piece — a complete partition.

java.line: results.add(new ArrayList<>(path));   // whole string consumed → record a COPY
java.explanation: Snapshot the list of pieces; the live path mutates on backtrack and would corrupt stored partitions.

java.line: for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {
java.explanation: Branch on the cut point: `end` is where the next piece ends, sweeping every possibility from start onward.

java.line: if (isPalindrome(s, start, end)) {            // prune: only cut on a palindrome
java.explanation: The pruning step — a non-palindromic prefix can never lead to a valid partition, so skip its whole subtree.
CHOOSE: commit `s[start..end]` (substring's end index is exclusive, hence end+1) as the current piece.

java.line: backtrack(s, end + 1, path, results);     // explore the remainder
java.explanation: Recurse from `end + 1` so the next piece starts right after this one — non-overlapping, gap-free tiling.
UN-CHOOSE: pop the piece so sibling `end` values start from the correct prefix.
Two-pointer palindrome test from both ends inward — O(length) per check (use a DP table to make it O(1)).

python.explanation: Whole string consumed → the path is a complete valid partition.

python.line: results.append(path[:])              # whole string consumed → record a COPY
python.explanation: `path[:]` snapshots; appending `path` stores a reference later pops mutate.
Branch on the cut point — `end` ranges over every possible end of the next piece.

python.line: if is_palindrome(start, end):        # prune: only cut on a palindrome
python.explanation: Prune non-palindromic prefixes immediately, killing whole dead subtrees.
CHOOSE: `s[start:end+1]` is the substring (slice end is exclusive, so end+1 includes s[end]).
EXPLORE from end+1 so the next piece begins right after this one.
UN-CHOOSE: remove the piece so the next sibling cut sees the original prefix.

diagrams.title: Choose / explore / un-choose on "aab"
diagrams.caption: Each downward edge commits a palindromic piece and advances start past it. The "ab" and "aab" prefixes fail the palindrome test, so those branches are pruned.

edgeCases.behavior: end=0: "a" is a palindrome → recurse from 1 == len → record ["a"]. Returns [["a"]].
Every substring of equal characters is a palindrome, so all 2² = 4 partitions are produced: [a,a,a], [a,aa], [aa,a], [aaa]. Worst-case branching.

pitfalls: Recursing from `start` or `end` instead of `end + 1` — causes overlapping pieces or a re-used character.
Using exclusive/inclusive end indices inconsistently — `substring(start, end+1)` / `s[start:end+1]` must include s[end].
Checking the palindrome only at the end instead of pruning per cut — explores dead subtrees needlessly.
Appending the live `path` instead of a copy — every stored partition mutates to the same list.

commonMistakes: Recursing from `start` or `end` rather than `end + 1`, producing overlapping or skipped characters.
Filtering palindromes at the leaf instead of pruning at each cut, wasting exponential work.
Storing the live `path` reference instead of a copy, so every partition collapses to the same list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursing from the wrong index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After taking the piece s[start..end], the next piece must begin at end+1. Recursing from `end` reuses s[end] in two pieces; recursing from `start` re-cuts already-placed characters.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if is_palindrome(start, end):
    path.append(s[start:end + 1])
    backtrack(end, path)        # reuses s[end] — overlap!
    path.pop()
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if is_palindrome(start, end):
    path.append(s[start:end + 1])
    backtrack(end + 1, path)    # next piece starts after this one
    path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Generate-all-then-filter instead of pruning
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Enumerating every cut and only checking palindromes at the leaf explores huge dead subtrees. Pruning at each cut (only descend when the prefix is a palindrome) kills those subtrees instantly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for end in range(start, len(s)):
    path.append(s[start:end + 1])     # take ANY prefix
    backtrack(end + 1, path)          # check palindromes only at the leaf
    path.pop()
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for end in range(start, len(s)):
    if is_palindrome(start, end):     # prune here
        path.append(s[start:end + 1])
        backtrack(end + 1, path)
        path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing the live path reference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `results.append(path)` stores the same list object; the pops on backtrack mutate it so every partition becomes identical. Snapshot with `path[:]`.

followupVariations.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
followupVariations.hint: Only the MINIMUM number of cuts is needed → pure DP: dp[i] = min cuts for s[0..i], using an isPalindrome[i][j] table. Don't enumerate partitions.

followupVariations.title: Word Break II
followupVariations.hint: Same cut-point backtracking, but the per-piece predicate is 'is in the dictionary' instead of 'is a palindrome'; memoise by start index to avoid recomputation.

followupVariations.title: Restore IP Addresses
followupVariations.hint: Partition into exactly 4 pieces, each a valid 0–255 octet → cut-point backtracking with a piece-count check and a per-octet validity prune.

followupVariations.title: Subsets
followupVariations.hint: Same choose/explore/un-choose skeleton — Subsets branches on element indices with no predicate; this branches on cut points with a palindrome predicate.

patternNote: Canonical Backtracking over cut points with a per-piece predicate (choose → explore → un-choose). Recognise it whenever you must enumerate ALL ways to split a sequence so each contiguous piece satisfies a test. The skeleton matches Subsets; the predicate prune and `end + 1` advance are the partition-specific pieces. Precomputing an isPalindrome[i][j] DP table (the dynamic-programming half) makes each check O(1).
